He was speaking at a business roundtable organised by the Bank Group in collaboration with the Japanese private sector in Tokyo on 12 November, during his second official visit to Japan as President. Dr Ould Tah outlined three investment priorities: promoting Africa's natural resources and creating greater value on the continent; developing the energy, transport and digital infrastructure essential for industrialisation; and harnessing Japanese technology and finance to support African businesses and bankable projects on the continent. Addressing a large gathering of Japanese business leaders and representatives of private financial institutions and development finance institutions (DFIs), Dr Ould Tah said, "Africa has the resources, markets and talent needed to become a major production hub. But this future will not be built solely on the export of raw materials." He invited them to forge a new generation of investment partnerships to transform African resources into added value, jobs and competitive industries.

Morocco, who had been declared champions after a Confederation of African Football (CAF) review, has now been confirmed as runners-up. "The Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) has upheld the appeal by the Senegalese Football Federation (FSF) against the Confederation of African Football (CAF) and the the Royal Moroccan Football Federation (FRMF, in French)," the CAS statement read. "The decision rendered by the CAF Appeal Board is set aside and the decision by the CAF Disciplinary Board is reinstated. Consequently, the result obtained at the end of the AFCON 2025 final is confirmed." The statement continued that it felt "the Referee' s decision to resume the match or to stop it fell definitively within his sole authority" and that his "decision was covered by the ‘field of play’ doctrine." The decision comes after a closed-doors hearing at CAS' headquarters in Lausanne in early October. Before the verdict was delivered, Morocco captain Achraf Hakimi posted a message on Instagram saying he would disagree with Senegal being stripped of the title because "its players fought so hard to win." "I respect the authorities responsible for football, but I firmly believe that what happens on the pitch should be the most important thing of all. Photograph: Courtesy of CPJ Africa Mentors, colleagues and friends: tributes paid to the ‘Eritrea 16’ who disappeared 25 years ago Families of journalists who vanished into state prisons on ‘Black Tuesday’ in 2001 do not know whether they are even still alive When Fisseha Yirgalem stepped on to the podium and began reading from a letter written to a man who may never hear it, the room full of journalists in Nairobi fell quiet. The Eritrean writer’s personal tribute to Amanuel Asrat , a poet, writer, and founder of Zemen newspaper, was not merely about an abstract human rights case but about her mentor, former colleague and friend whose life had in effect been erased by the authoritarian state of Eritrea. Asrat is one of 16 journalists who disappeared into Eritrea’s prison system 25 years ago on Black Tuesday – 18 September 2001 – when the government shut down all of the newspapers in the country.

stories.title: One in four women globally unable to refuse sex within marriage, says UN
stories.summary: Seven countries in Africa expressly exempt husbands from prosecution for marital rape, including Côte d’Ivoire, Ethiopia and South Sudan. Photograph: Frank Dejongh/Unicef One in four women globally unable to refuse sex within marriage, says UN Almost half of women in west and central Africa cannot withhold consent, with girls worst affected, UNFPA finds One in four women around the world have no power of consent if their husband or partner demands sex, according to a UN report. In west and central Africa, almost half of women (45%) are not able to say no in their own marriage, while a third of women (33%) in east and southern Africa and in Arab states face the same predicament. In Latin America and the Caribbean, one in 10 women are not able to refuse sex, said the report by the UN Population Fund ( UNFPA ) published on Thursday.

Photograph: Danish Siddiqui/Reuters Fears grow that US will put Nobel-winning judge under sanctions after Myanmar genocide ruling A ruling against Myanmar could set precedent for court’s judgment on Israel’s actions in Gaza Fears are growing that the US could impose sanctions on judges at the international court of justice, including this year’s Nobel peace prize winner, Navi Pillay , if the court rules on Thursday that the Myanmar government committed genocide against the Rohingya. ‘They showed no mercy’: mapping the Rohingya villages being erased by rebel forces Read more The ICJ has never found a state responsible for committing genocide, and a significant factor in previous cases has been how to prove “intent” in a crime defined as acts committed with the “intent to destroy, in whole or in part” a national, ethnical, racial or religious group. Lawyers representing Rohingya survivors say patterns of behaviour by Myanmar’s military, including killing people as they fled, show clear attempts to destroy the group during assaults on Rakhine state in 2016 and 2017. It is the role of independent judges to interpret the genocide convention.

stories.title: Can a US-backed mineral highway bring peace and prosperity to DR Congo?
stories.summary: Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, The Lobito Corridor links DR Congo's mineral-rich south to Angola's Atlantic coast through the Benguela Railway and the Port of Lobito By Akisa Wandera BBC Africa ,Â Reporting from Lobito Published 18 November 2026 As trains carrying thousands of tonnes of copper from the Democratic Republic of Congo roar through her community, 20-year-old Manuela Julia is not thinking about critical minerals or billion-dollar investments. She is thinking about getting around more easily. The railway runs through Catumbela, near the Angolan city of Lobito, on the Atlantic coast. For Julia, it has made travelling cheaper and more convenient. "Before, I had to use a taxi, which is much more expensive. Now it is cheaper and easier to travel," she says.

stories.title: European Commission accused of sugarcoating figures to release funds to Egypt
stories.summary: Ursula von der Leyen and Abdel Fatah al-Sisi after a meeting in Cairo in March 2024. Photograph: Stavros Ioannides/PIO/AFP/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Ursula von der Leyen and Abdel Fatah al-Sisi after a meeting in Cairo in March 2024. Photograph: Stavros Ioannides/PIO/AFP/Getty Images European Commission accused of sugarcoating figures to release funds to Egypt Leaked documents raise questions about claims Egypt met welfare targets to qualify for €2.5bn in loans The European Commission has been accused of sugarcoating figures to enable it to release funds to Egypt under a landmark pact with the authoritarian government of Abdel Fatah al-Sisi. The charge relates to a €7.4bn deal promised by Ursula von der Leyen , the European Commission president, to al-Sisi on a high-profile visit to Cairo in 2024. The three-year “strategic and comprehensive partnership” was intended to bolster Egypt’s shaky economy, deter migrants from coming to Europe and shore up a region reeling from the 7 October attacks and Israel’s war on Gaza.
